title: The cloud-wave dispatch step exceeds Cloudflare Workflows' 10-minute step limit, killing its own supervisor
description:
THE defect behind every failed fan-out run, found by querying the Workflow instance directly rather than inferring from the run record.

Both live runs errored identically:

  GET /accounts/<acc>/workflows/ticks-run/instances/<run_id>
  status: errored
  error:  {"message": "Execution timed out after 600000ms", "name": "Error"}
  last step: cloud:dispatch:0-1

600000ms is 10 minutes: Cloudflare Workflows' per-step EXECUTION limit. superviseCloudWave calls dispatchWave inside a single step.do(), and dispatchWave BLOCKS until every container in the wave settles — wait_timeout_ms is now the worker budget plus the push margin, i.e. up to 90 minutes. A step that waits longer than 10 minutes cannot survive, so the cloud-wave path is architecturally guaranteed to kill its own supervisor on any wave that takes more than ten minutes. Which is every real wave.

WHAT THIS EXPLAINS, all previously misread as other things:
- The run record stays 'running' forever while nothing supervises it. Only the Workflow updates that column, and the Workflow is dead. run_9e40b956 sat at 'running' for 97 minutes with its supervisor gone since roughly minute 10.
- Containers keep working, orphaned. run_9e40b956's three workers went on making model calls until 14:02 — long after the supervisor died at ~13:32 — and were never collected, never merged, never torn down.
- 'lease: null' on a live run: nothing was left alive to renew it.
- Run 1's permanent 'stopping' state. A hard stop asks the Workflow to wind down; there was no Workflow left to do it.
- Why tick ys3 cost seven runs to diagnose. Every one of those runs ALSO had a dead supervisor, so the dispatch-outcome record it was trying to read was written by a step that never completed.

NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH 5fg, because it is counter-intuitive: raising the worker budget from 30 to 90 minutes made this WORSE, not better. A longer wave is a longer blocking step. 5fg is still correct — killing agents at 29 minutes was real — but the two changes have to land together for either to help.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX: dispatch and waiting must be separate steps, with the wait spread across many bounded steps rather than one long one. supervisePass already does exactly this for the single-sandbox path — MAX_OBSERVATIONS with a stretching pollDelay, each observation a short step — and that path has run for hours without hitting this. Follow it rather than inventing a second pattern: dispatch in one step, then observe the wave across bounded steps, reconciling from the durable layer each time so a resumed or retried step re-derives state instead of holding it in memory.

Nothing in cloud/factory/src references the 10-minute cap today. Whatever the fix, name the limit as a documented constant with the platform behaviour written down, so the next person adding a step does not rediscover it in production.

acceptance_criteria: A cloud wave whose containers run for an hour completes with its Workflow still alive: the run record reaches a terminal state, branches are collected, and 'tk cloud status' never shows 'running' for a run whose supervisor is gone. The 10-minute step limit is a named, documented constant. Proven by a live run.
closed_reason: Completed: a cloud wave is now watched across bounded Workflow legs (each its own step, 420s of waiting against the 600s cap) instead of one blocking step that killed its own supervisor. Follows supervisePass's existing pattern rather than a second one. State crosses legs in checkpointed step results and liveness is re-derived by reconcileWave every leg, so a retried or replayed step re-decides identically — no Date.now(), no closures. Cancel cadence, gyl's revoke-before-teardown ordering, teardown on every path, manifestRecorder and ys3's writeWaveOutcomes all preserved and re-tested. The 10-minute cap is now a named constant in cloud/factory/src/workflow-limits.ts.
